what: Predicting Class Membership from an Auxiliary Variable
title: Auxiliary Analyses for Random-Effects Mixture Meta-Analysis
text: far, examined whether latent classes differ auxiliary variables. can also reverse question: Can auxiliary variables predict latent class membership? example, suppose expect true population effect zero, research effect first introduced, early studies reported large positive effects due publication bias (/questionable research practices). case, study characteristic z might represent “year publication”. theory implies hypothesis z causes class membership. test hypothesis, can use pseudo_class() repeatedly draw plausible class assignments posterior probabilities, fit logistic regression dataset, pool regression estimates. regression estimates association z log odds belonging class 2 rather class 1. negative coefficient indicates higher values z associated greater odds class 1 membership. see effect significant; thus, plausible publication year explains different classes. present model can use logistic regression two classes. two classes, multinomial logistic regression appropriate, e.g.:
code: # Predict latent class membership from an auxiliary variable set.seed(783) pred <- pseudo_class(   x = fit,   model = glm(     I(as.integer(class) == 2L) ~ z,     data = data,     family = binomial()   ),   data = data.frame(z = dat$z),   m = 10 ) pred #>          term   estimate std.error statistic       df      p.value #> 1 (Intercept) -0.6089003 0.1921151 -3.169455 123.7412 1.924902e-03 #> 2           z  0.8992796 0.1891752  4.753687  86.3312 7.913785e-06 pred <- pseudo_class(   x = fit,   model = function(data) {     nnet::multinom(       factor(class) ~ z,       data = data,       trace = FALSE     )   },   data = data.frame(z = dat$z),   m = 10 )

title: Calculate Surprisal Using Kernel Density Estimation — surprisal
code: set.seed(123)  x <- rnorm(1000) y <- c(0, 1, 2, 3)  # Individual surprisal values surprisal(x, y, aggregate = FALSE) #> [1] 0.8767707 1.4248554 2.7872109 5.6401511  # Total surprisal surprisal(x, y) #> [1] 10.72899  # Mean surprisal surprisal(x, y, aggregate = "mean") #> [1] 2.682247
